source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: For most models in Silver, the minimum wall thickness you can use is 0.6 mm for the gloss finish and 0.8 mm for the high gloss finish. However, when making something small such as the band of a ring, the wall thickness should be at least 1 mm.
claim: Minimum wall thickness for silver lost-wax casting is 0.6 mm for gloss finish, 0.8 mm for high gloss finish. For ring bands specifically, minimum wall thickness should be at least 1 mm.
notes: Materialise distinguishes between gloss and high gloss finish, implying finishing affects minimum wall. Ring band minimum is higher due to wear fragility, not casting limitation.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Gold | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: For most models in Gold, the minimum wall thickness you can use is 0.8 mm. However, when making something small such as the band of a ring, the wall thickness should be at least 1 mm.
claim: Minimum wall thickness for gold lost-wax casting is 0.8 mm. For ring bands specifically, minimum wall thickness should be at least 1 mm.
notes: Same ring band minimum as silver, but higher general minimum (0.8 vs 0.6). This suggests the ring band constraint is wear-driven, not casting-driven.

source.title: How to Prepare a Jewelry CAD Model for Wax Printing and Casting

location.section: Minimum Wall Thickness and Feature Size for Castable Models

excerpt: Our general guidance is a minimum wall thickness of about 0.8 mm for sterling silver and 0.6 to 0.7 mm for gold and platinum, with 1.0 mm a much safer target on larger surfaces like wide bands and signet tops.
claim: Minimum wall thickness for sterling silver is approximately 0.8 mm, for gold and platinum 0.6-0.7 mm, with 1.0 mm recommended for larger surfaces.
notes: Practitioner source. Silver minimum (0.8) is higher than Materialise (0.6). This may reflect a more conservative production safety margin or different wax/resin printing process.

location.section: Wall thickness: not too thin, not too heavy

excerpt: Minimum wall thickness guidelines: Silver & bronze: min. 0.8 mm. Gold: min. 0.6 mm. Bridges & connectors: min. 1.0 - 1.2 mm.
claim: Minimum wall thickness for silver and bronze is 0.8 mm, for gold 0.6 mm, for bridges and connectors 1.0-1.2 mm.
notes: Independent practitioner confirms 0.8 mm for silver. Adds bridges/connectors category at 1.0-1.2 mm. Also warns against overly thick sections causing shrinkage voids.

source.title: Minimum Wall Thickness for Jewelry CAM Printing and Casting

excerpt: Around 0.7 mm wall thickness. Keep shell walls even and avoid random thick spots. Thin, consistent shells burn out more predictably.
claim: Hollow shell wall thickness baseline is approximately 0.7 mm for castable wax/resin printing.
notes: Specifically for hollow shells, not solid walls. References Formlabs castable wax guide for the 0.7 mm number.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: The smallest features in your design should be at least 0.35 mm in diameter and 0.4 mm in height and attached to a solid surface. Details this small are suitable for delicate projects such as micro pavé settings. Because Silver is not a very strong material, longer features such as rods or prongs (in mesh-like structures) should be at least 0.8 mm in diameter.
claim: Minimum feature size for silver is 0.35 mm diameter and 0.4 mm height, attached to solid surface. Rods/prongs in mesh-like structures should be at least 0.8 mm diameter.
notes: Distinguishes between general features and structural features (rods/prongs). The 0.8 mm prong minimum is about structural integrity, not casting resolution.

source.title: How to Prepare a Jewelry CAD Model for Wax Printing and Casting

location.section: Minimum Wall Thickness and Feature Size for Castable Models

excerpt: Raised lettering, milgrain, and filigree should generally be at least 0.3 to 0.4 mm wide and tall, or they either fail to print or disappear the moment the piece is polished. Engraved or recessed details should be at least 0.2 to 0.3 mm deep so they survive finishing.
claim: Raised features should be 0.3-0.4 mm wide and tall. Engraved/recessed details should be 0.2-0.3 mm deep to survive finishing.
notes: Key insight: features must survive polishing, not just casting. Engraving depth is about post-finishing survival, not casting capability.

excerpt: We recommend a minimum draft angle of 7°, a maximum depth of 0.5mm, and a minimum width of 0.75mm for all CAD/wax engraving.
claim: For CAD/wax engraving: minimum draft angle 7°, maximum depth 0.5 mm, minimum width 0.75 mm.
notes: Only source with specific engraving draft angle and width. Note: maximum depth (not minimum) suggests deeper engravings cause casting issues.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: For embossing or engraving details such as text, we advise you to keep a maximum height/depth-to-width ratio of 1:1. Also, keep in mind the minimum wall thickness of 0.35 mm.
claim: Engraving/embossing should maintain maximum height/depth-to-width ratio of 1:1. Minimum wall thickness of 0.35 mm applies.
notes: Ratio constraint is about aspect ratio, not absolute depth. Combined with 0.35 mm minimum, implies a 0.35 mm deep engraving needs 0.35 mm width.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: We advise a minimum gap of 0.3 mm. If it is impossible to increase the gap in your design, you can consider fusing the features if their separation is unnecessary.
claim: Minimum clearance between parts is 0.3 mm to prevent fusion during casting.
notes: Same value for gold (src-0002 confirms). Root cause: plaster may not fully flow into gaps < 0.3 mm, creating thin mold walls that break during metal pour.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: You need to incorporate multiple holes or slots so that we can get rid of any unprinted wax resin. Make as many holes or slots as you possibly can. We recommend making two or more holes or slots. The holes should have a diameter larger than 1.5 mm.
claim: Hollow models require 2+ evacuation holes with diameter > 1.5 mm for wax resin removal.
notes: Same value for gold (src-0002 confirms). Holes must be spread out equally, e.g. on opposite ends.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

location.section: Influence of finishes on level of detail

excerpt: Polished: erode 0.05 to 0.075 mm. Corundum blasted (Matte): erode 0.10 to 0.15 mm. Brushed: erode 0.10 to 0.15 mm. Hand polished: erode 0.10 to 0.15 mm.
claim: Finishing erosion by type: Polished (magnetic tumbler) 0.05-0.075 mm, Sandblasted 0.10-0.15 mm, Brushed 0.10-0.15 mm, Hand polished 0.10-0.15 mm.
notes: Critical for geometry validation: features must account for finishing erosion. Hand polishing removes 2-3x more material than magnetic tumbling.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: As a rule, we can't file, sand or polish cavities, and small sharp edges will be rounded off. Also, complex internal, mesh-like structures are impossible to reach.
claim: Cavities and complex internal structures cannot be polished. Sharp edges will be rounded off.
notes: This is a heuristic, not a measurable geometric property. Accessibility depends on tool size and geometry.

source.title: How to Prepare a Jewelry CAD Model for Wax Printing and Casting

excerpt: The combined effect is small but real: roughly 1.5 to 2 percent for silver and gold alloys, with platinum on the higher end. The usual fix is to scale the model up by about 1.5 to 2 percent before printing.
claim: Casting shrinkage for silver and gold is approximately 1.5-2%, for platinum on the higher end. Model should be scaled up by 1.5-2% to compensate.
notes: Practitioner source. Shrinkage is linear. Applied as scale factor before printing.

source.title: Understanding Casting Shrinkage in Jewelry Manufacturing

location.section: Shrinkage Rates for Common Jewelry Metals

excerpt: 14K Gold: Approximately 1.5-1.7% shrinkage. 18K Gold: Around 1.3-1.5% shrinkage. Sterling Silver: Typically 1.8-2.1% shrinkage. Platinum: Generally 1.8-2.0% shrinkage. Brass: Usually 1.5-1.8% shrinkage.
claim: Linear shrinkage rates: 14K gold 1.5-1.7%, 18K gold 1.3-1.5%, sterling silver 1.8-2.1%, platinum 1.8-2.0%, brass 1.5-1.8%.
notes: More granular than src-0003. Sterling silver (1.8-2.1%) is slightly higher than eCadCam's 1.5-2%. Alloy composition affects shrinkage.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

excerpt: Standard accuracy ±5% (with a lower limit of ±0.35 mm). Layer thickness 0.016 mm. Maximum part dimensions 88 x 88 x 125 mm.
claim: Standard accuracy is ±5% with lower limit of ±0.35 mm. Maximum part dimensions 88×88×125 mm. Layer thickness 0.016 mm.
notes: Same values for gold (src-0002). The ±5% with ±0.35 mm lower limit means small parts have relatively large tolerance bands.

source.title: The Engineer's Guide to Investment Casting Tolerances

excerpt: ISO 8062-3 defines CT grades. For silica sol investment casting: CT4-CT6 production range. CT4 at 0-10mm = ±0.13mm. CT5 at 25-40mm = ±0.23mm. CT6 at 40-63mm = ±0.35mm.
claim: ISO 8062-3 CT grades for investment casting: CT4-CT6 typical. CT4: ±0.13mm at 0-10mm. CT5: ±0.23mm at 25-40mm. CT6: ±0.35mm at 40-63mm.
notes: Industrial investment casting, not jewelry-specific. Jewelry lost-wax from printed patterns may differ. Materialise's ±5%/±0.35mm is roughly CT6 for small parts.

source.title: How to Prepare a Jewelry CAD Model for Wax Printing and Casting

excerpt: We recommend modeling prongs slightly oversized, around 0.9 to 1.1 mm in diameter for a typical center stone, and tapering them only above the seat so there is enough metal at the base.
claim: Prong diameter should be 0.9-1.1 mm for center stones, tapered only above the seat.
notes: Prongs are the most failure-prone feature. Leave extra material for setter to trim. Bezel walls 0.4-0.6 mm at top, thicker toward base.

source.title: How to Prepare a Jewelry CAD Model for Wax Printing and Casting

excerpt: For bezels and channel settings, keep the wall that will be pushed over the stone between 0.4 and 0.6 mm at the top and thicker toward the base. Pavé fields need consistent spacing with enough metal between holes, usually no less than 0.3 mm, so beads can be raised without breaking through.
claim: Bezel/channel setting walls: 0.4-0.6 mm at top, thicker toward base. Pavé spacing between holes: minimum 0.3 mm.
notes: Bezel wall thickness is about stone-setting, not casting. Pavé spacing is about metal between holes.

source.title: Minimum Wall Thickness for Jewelry CAM Printing and Casting

location.section: Thick Sections Are a Different Kind of Problem

excerpt: Formlabs' castable wax guide recommends reviewing any section thicker than 4 mm for shelling. For hollow shells, they recommend around 0.7 mm wall thickness plus drain holes.
claim: Sections thicker than 4 mm should be reviewed for shelling. Hollow shell walls should be ~0.7 mm with drain holes.
notes: Thick sections cause expansion stress and ash residue during burnout. This is a wax/resin printing constraint, not a metal casting constraint.

location.section: Wall thickness: not too thin, not too heavy

excerpt: Avoid unnecessary bulk. Overly thick sections cool unevenly and create shrinkage voids inside the metal. Aim for consistent wall thickness throughout your design.
claim: Overly thick sections cause uneven cooling and shrinkage voids. Consistent wall thickness is recommended.
notes: No specific number for maximum solid thickness. Confirms thick sections cause shrinkage voids.

source.title: Design Guidelines for Silver | Lost-Wax Casting

location.section: Nested objects, hinged and interlocking parts

excerpt: Nested objects (objects floating within another object), hinged parts, and interlocking parts, such as chains, cannot be made with lost wax casting. The reason is that support structures have to be removed before being cast in Silver.
claim: Nested objects, hinged parts, and interlocking parts cannot be made with lost wax casting.
notes: Same for gold (src-0002). This is a hard process limitation — supports must be removed before casting.

source.title: Measure Thickness Tool in MeshInspector Explained

excerpt: Rays calculates thickness by casting rays along surface normals and measuring the distance to the opposite side of the mesh. Spheres estimates thickness using inscribed and circumscribed spheres at surface points.
claim: Two methods for mesh thickness measurement: (1) Ray casting along surface normals to opposite side, (2) Sphere-based estimation using inscribed/circumscribed spheres.
notes: Ray method is fast, best for clean geometry. Sphere method is more robust for complex/curved shapes but slower. Both are candidate algorithms for Sculptura's measurement layer.

excerpt: We would advise structural and external walls to have a minimum metal thickness of 0.8mm with smaller elements such as claws or small setting bezels to have a minimum metal thickness of 0.5mm.
claim: Structural/external walls: minimum 0.8 mm. Claws/small setting bezels: minimum 0.5 mm.
notes: Confirms 0.8 mm consensus for walls. Adds 0.5 mm for small elements (claws/bezels). Earring posts will not be printed — must be soldered on after.

excerpt: Structural and external walls must have minimum metal thickness of 0.8mm.
claim: Structural and external walls: minimum 0.8 mm metal thickness.
notes: Third manufacturer confirming 0.8 mm. Stuller uses 'must' (requirement), Cooksongold uses 'would advise' (recommendation).

excerpt: Raised text must be 0.30mm thickness at a minimum and no more than 0.60mm high with a spacing of 0.30mm between letters. Recessed text must be 0.30mm thickness at a minimum and no more than 0.50mm deep with a spacing of 0.30mm between letters. We would also recommend using a negative draft angle (taper).
claim: Raised text: min 0.30 mm thickness, max 0.60 mm height, 0.30 mm spacing. Recessed text: min 0.30 mm width, max 0.50 mm depth, 0.30 mm spacing, negative draft angle recommended.
notes: Very specific. Max height 0.60 mm for raised, max depth 0.50 mm for recessed. Negative draft angle (taper) recommended for recessed.

excerpt: Raised letters need a minimum metal thickness of 0.3mm. Raised letters should not be higher than 0.6mm above the surface. Minimum spacing of 0.3mm between raised letters. Recessed letters must have a minimum width of 0.3mm. Depth of recessed letters can be no more than double the width.
claim: Raised letters: min 0.3 mm thickness, max 0.6 mm height, 0.3 mm spacing. Recessed letters: min 0.3 mm width, max depth = 2× width.
notes: Confirms Cooksongold values exactly (0.3/0.6/0.3). Stuller adds depth-to-width ratio of 2:1 for recessed (vs Materialise's 1:1). Stuller requires fillets on all edges.

excerpt: Small holes should be avoided as they will cause issues during the process. Holes should be no smaller than 0.50mm at a minimum. Fill the holes during the CAD process and if you do need to create pilot holes for setting then use a conical/spherical shape to create a guide for a drill to be used once cast.
claim: Minimum hole diameter: 0.50 mm. Pilot holes should use conical/spherical shape, width larger than depth.
notes: Root cause: small holes cause investment relocation during casting. Conical/spherical pilot holes are better than cylindrical.

location.section: Pilot Holes and Divots / General openings rule

excerpt: All openings in a design should be a minimum of 0.4mm to avoid being filled in during casting or causing investment relocation. The depth of the opening can be no more than double the diameter.
claim: Minimum opening: 0.4 mm. Maximum depth: 2× diameter.
notes: Stuller 0.4 mm vs Cooksongold 0.5 mm. Both cite investment relocation as root cause. Stuller adds 2:1 depth-to-diameter ratio.

excerpt: If you do have a sharp external edge, we would recommend either thickening the edge to 0.30mm or using the fillet tool to create a soft 0.30mm radius.
claim: Sharp edges should be thickened to 0.30 mm or filleted with 0.30 mm radius.
notes: Sharp edges do not print well. Better to have too much material and sharpen during finishing.

excerpt: The prong must overlap the girdle of the stone. The seat should not cut deeper than 25% of the prong. Minimum prong diameter for pinpoint: 0.45mm. Minimum distance between gallery rails/bearings: 0.4mm. Minimum channel wall thickness: 0.4mm.
claim: Prong seat depth: max 25% of prong. Pinpoint prong diameter: min 0.45 mm. Gallery rail spacing: min 0.4 mm. Channel wall: min 0.4 mm.
notes: Very detailed. Stuller uses 'must' for most rules. Bezel wall min 0.45 mm. Bead size 0.4-0.5 mm. Milgrain min 0.3 mm above finger rail.

excerpt: We recommend the minimum shank thicknesses pictured below because, on average, production can remove up to 0.2mm of metal. Design elements and scroll work should have a minimum metal thickness of 0.5mm. All design elements should overlap each other by 0.15mm.
claim: Production can remove up to 0.2 mm of metal during finishing. Design elements: min 0.5 mm. Element overlap: min 0.15 mm.
notes: Stuller's 0.2 mm erosion is at the high end of Materialise's 0.05-0.15 mm range. This may include filing + polishing, not just tumbling.

excerpt: Stones must have a minimum clearance of 0.5mm from the culet to the finger rail.
claim: Stone culet to finger rail: minimum 0.5 mm clearance.
notes: Prevents stone from touching finger. Geometry-specific: measurable from mesh if stone position is known.

excerpt: Unfortunately, we cannot process hollow pieces. To get around this you may be able to cast two halves and solder/weld the two pieces together. The same applies to interlocking/multiple pieces.
claim: Hollow pieces are not supported. Interlocking/multiple pieces not supported. Must be cast as separate parts and assembled.
notes: Cooksongold does NOT support hollow pieces at all, while Materialise DOES support hollow with evacuation holes. This is a manufacturer-specific difference, not a process limitation.

excerpt: Designs must fit within the maximum size of 30mm x 50mm x 70mm. Finishing can remove approximately 0.1mm. We apply a scaling increase to cover shrinkage.
claim: Max part size: 30×50×70 mm. Finishing removes ~0.1 mm. Shrinkage compensated by scaling.
notes: Much smaller build envelope than Materialise (88×88×125). Finishing erosion 0.1 mm matches Materialise's mid-range. Shrinkage value not specified numerically.

source.title: Shrinking sphere: A parallel algorithm for computing the thickness of 3D objects

excerpt: In the ray method, the thickness at a point p on a surface is given by a ray shot from p in a direction opposite to the local outward normal. The Euclidean distance d between p and another point q corresponds to the thickness. This definition is ambiguous if the two surfaces containing p and q are not parallel, because the thickness values at p and q will be different. The sphere method returns consistent results for any object. The thickness at a point p on a surface is given by the diameter of the maximum inscribed sphere (MIS) touching p.
claim: Two thickness measurement methods: (1) Ray method — casts ray along inward normal, measures distance to opposite surface. Ambiguous for non-parallel surfaces. (2) Sphere method — diameter of maximum inscribed sphere (MIS) touching the point. Consistent for any shape. MIS locus corresponds to medial axis.

value.sphere_method: consistent, MIS-based, corresponds to medial axis

notes: Key insight: ray method gives different thickness values at p and q when surfaces are non-parallel. Sphere method is consistent. For jewelry (curved surfaces, rings), sphere method is more appropriate. Shrinking sphere algorithm converges in ~5 iterations, can process 2M polygons in minutes with GPU.

source.title: Shrinking sphere: A parallel algorithm for computing the thickness of 3D objects

excerpt: Thickness is a basic parameter in machine-part design. The thickness of individual walls and ribs is important for calculating allowable stresses and strains. In additive manufacturing, wall thickness is a crucial factor affecting part production.
claim: Wall thickness is a crucial factor in additive manufacturing, affecting production time and cost.
notes: Academic confirmation that wall thickness is a primary geometric parameter for manufacturing validation.

excerpt: Minimum Wall Thickness: 1 mm (0.039 in). Supported walls are connected to two or more sides and are thick enough to support the model. Thinner walls may warp or curl during the sintering process due to thermal stresses.
claim: DMLS minimum wall thickness: 1.0 mm for supported walls. Thinner walls may warp or curl due to thermal stresses.
notes: DMLS requires thicker walls than lost-wax (1.0 vs 0.8 mm). Root cause: thermal stress during sintering, not casting fill. Supported vs unsupported distinction matters.

excerpt: Debossed Details: Minimum depth 0.5 mm (0.02 in). Embossed Details: Minimum height 0.5 mm.
claim: DMLS minimum debossed detail depth: 0.5 mm. Minimum embossed detail height: 0.5 mm.
notes: DMLS requires deeper features than lost-wax (0.5 vs 0.2-0.5 mm). Quality depends on orientation — place details away from overhanging faces requiring support.

excerpt: Minimum Clearance: 0.5 mm (0.02 in). Clearance is the distance between two moving parts on hinges, joints, mating parts.
claim: DMLS minimum clearance between moving parts: 0.5 mm.
notes: DMLS needs more clearance than lost-wax (0.5 vs 0.3 mm). This is for moving/assembled parts, not fused parts.

excerpt: Minimum Hole Size: 0.5 mm (0.02 in). Depending on orientation, circular holes can resolve as ovals — if higher accuracy is required, printing the center mark and post-machining is recommended.
claim: DMLS minimum hole diameter: 0.5 mm. Circular holes may resolve as ovals depending on orientation.
notes: Same as Cooksongold lost-wax (0.5 mm). Orientation affects hole roundness — DMLS-specific issue. Post-machining recommended for tight tolerances.

excerpt: General Tolerance: ±0.3% (min ±0.3 mm). Standard production tolerance is ±0.3% of feature size with a minimum of ±0.3 mm.
claim: DMLS general tolerance: ±0.3% with minimum ±0.3 mm.
notes: Tighter than Materialise lost-wax (±5%/±0.35 mm). DMLS is more dimensionally accurate than lost-wax casting.

excerpt: Metal 3D printed parts are shot peened to a surface uniform roughness of 200 - 400 Ra after support removal.
claim: DMLS as-printed surface roughness: 200-400 Ra after shot peening.
notes: DMLS as-printed surface is rough. Jewelry would require significant post-processing (filing, polishing, tumbling). 200-400 Ra is much rougher than cast surfaces.

excerpt: Due to shrinkage on solidification, and the polishing and finishing process, your final casting will be slightly smaller by about 1-3% so you need to allow for this in your master pattern. Models don't necessarily shrink uniformly.
claim: Total shrinkage (solidification + polishing) is approximately 1-3%. Shrinkage is not uniform — varies by geometry.
notes: Third source for shrinkage. Wider range (1-3%) includes polishing reduction. Notes non-uniformity — important for Sculptura: uniform scale factor is an approximation.

source.title: Introduction to Casting for 3D Printed Jewelry Patterns

excerpt: Fine meshes can be printed with a wire diameter as thin as 0.3 mm. Printed filigree is fragile and easily damaged by support removal. Design filigree parts to be as self-supporting as possible.
claim: Minimum filigree wire diameter: 0.3 mm for Castable Wax Resin. Filigree is fragile and easily damaged by support removal.

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: This is a printing capability, not a casting constraint. The 0.3 mm wire can be printed but may not survive casting or finishing. Confirms Materialise's 0.35 mm minimum feature size as a more conservative production target.

source.title: Introduction to Casting for 3D Printed Jewelry Patterns

excerpt: Parts thicker than 4 mm should be shelled, and drain holes must be added to allow resin to flush out of the hollow interior. Uncured resin will not burn out cleanly, resulting in ash residue defects. Formlabs recommends 0.7 mm thick walls for hollow shells printed in Castable Wax Resin.
claim: Parts thicker than 4 mm should be shelled. Hollow shell walls: 0.7 mm. Drain holes required for resin removal.

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: Confirms Saqlain Bullion's 4 mm threshold (which cited Formlabs). 0.7 mm hollow shell matches Saqlain Bullion. Root cause: expansion forces on investment during burnout, ash residue from uncured resin.

excerpt: DMLS/SLM: 50°. Additional support might be necessary for sintering in binder jetting and metal extrusion.
claim: DMLS/SLM maximum overhang angle without support: 50° from horizontal.
notes: Overhang measured from horizontal (build plate). Surfaces angled less than 50° from horizontal need support. This is a DMLS-specific constraint — not applicable to lost-wax casting. Geometric observable: surface normal relative to build direction.

excerpt: DMLS/SLM: 0.5 mm. Consider eliminating the overhang by adding a 45° chamfer under the unsupported edges.
claim: DMLS/SLM maximum unsupported edge length: 0.5 mm. Use 45° chamfer to eliminate overhang.
notes: Very short — 0.5 mm is the max overhang before support is needed. This is much stricter than polymer printing.

excerpt: DMLS/SLM: 8:1. Extra stability can be added to tall features using support ribs (similar to injection molding).
claim: DMLS/SLM maximum aspect ratio for features: 8:1. Use support ribs for tall features.
notes: Height-to-width ratio. Important for prongs and raised features.

excerpt: DMLS/SLM: 0.4 mm. Binder Jetting: 1.0 mm. Metal Extrusion: 1.0 mm.
claim: DMLS/SLM minimum wall thickness: 0.4 mm. Binder jetting: 1.0 mm. Metal extrusion: 1.0 mm.
notes: Hubs reports 0.4 mm for DMLS — lower than Forge Labs' 1.0 mm. This may be the theoretical minimum vs production recommendation. Forge Labs specifies supported walls at 1.0 mm.

excerpt: DMLS/SLM: Ø1.5 mm. For holes that are not aligned along the build direction, consider using a teardrop shape instead to avoid the need for support.
claim: DMLS/SLM minimum hole diameter: 1.5 mm. Use teardrop shape for non-vertical holes to avoid support.
notes: Much larger than lost-wax (0.4-0.5 mm). Teardrop shape prevents support material inside holes. Orientation-dependent — vertical holes can be smaller.

location.section: Design rules — Minimum feature size / Minimum detail size

excerpt: Minimum feature size DMLS/SLM: 0.6 mm. Minimum detail size DMLS/SLM: 0.4 mm. Isolated features are more prone to failure during printing or handling than wall sections.
claim: DMLS/SLM minimum feature size: 0.6 mm (isolated features). Minimum detail size: 0.4 mm (engraved/embossed).
notes: Distinguishes feature size (isolated pins/features) from detail size (engraved/embossed). Forge Labs says 0.5 mm for both — slight discrepancy.

excerpt: Out of the printer, the surface roughness of the produced parts is relatively high for most engineering applications, so post-processing is necessary. Standard RA 10 μm of as-printed DMLS/SLM.
claim: DMLS/SLM as-printed surface roughness: ~10 μm Ra standard.
notes: Different from Forge Labs' 200-400 Ra (shot peened). Hubs reports as-printed, Forge Labs reports post-shot-peen. Both are much rougher than cast surfaces.

source.title: Complete Guide to Direct Metal 3D Printing for Jewelry

excerpt: Sterling Silver Ag925: 98 to 99% density, moderate roughness, widely available. Gold 18K: 99.5%+ density, requires polishing, limited suppliers. Platinum Pt950: 99%+ density, requires polishing, specialized suppliers.
claim: DMLS jewelry materials: Sterling silver (Ag925) 98-99% density, widely available. Gold 18K 99.5%+ density, limited suppliers. Platinum Pt950 99%+ density, specialized suppliers.
notes: DMLS density is lower than cast (99.5%+ for casting). Silver is most available for DMLS. Gold powder costs 20-40% more than bullion.

source.title: Complete Guide to Direct Metal 3D Printing for Jewelry

excerpt: Binder jetting is faster and less expensive per part than laser-based methods, but the sintering step introduces 15 to 20 percent shrinkage that must be accounted for in the digital model. The final density is also typically lower than laser-processed parts, at around 95 to 98 percent versus 99+ percent.
claim: Binder jetting shrinkage: 15-20%. Density: 95-98% (vs 99%+ for DMLS/SLM).
notes: Binder jetting shrinkage (15-20%) is 10x higher than lost-wax casting (1.5-2%). This is a different process with very different compensation requirements.

source.title: Complete Guide to Direct Metal 3D Printing for Jewelry

excerpt: Typical build parameters for 18K gold include laser power of 100 to 200 watts, scan speed of 200 to 800 millimeters per second, and layer thickness of 20 to 30 microns. A single ring built in 18K gold takes approximately 3 to 8 hours of machine time.
claim: DMLS 18K gold build: laser 100-200W, scan 200-800 mm/s, layer 20-30 μm. Single ring: 3-8 hours machine time.
notes: Build time 3-8 hours per ring is much slower than resin printing. Layer thickness 20-30 μm is finer than typical DMLS (50 μm).

source.title: Complete Guide to Direct Metal 3D Printing for Jewelry

excerpt: Printed surfaces have a characteristic granular texture from the partially fused powder particles on the surface. Achieving jewelry-grade surface quality requires progressive steps of grinding, filing, sanding (through grits from 220 to 2000), and polishing.
claim: DMLS as-printed surface has granular texture. Jewelry-grade finish requires grinding, filing, sanding (220-2000 grit), and polishing.
notes: Much more post-processing than lost-wax casting. The granular texture is from partially fused powder particles. Sanding through 220-2000 grit is a multi-step process.

source.title: Metal AM Design: Strategies for Effective Powder Removal

excerpt: By incorporating powder removal canals (PRCs) within the structure, you can connect internal voids to the exterior, allowing un-melted powder to flow out post-printing. The PRCs, designed as cylindrical channels, are strategically placed to connect neighboring voids, facilitating powder evacuation.
claim: DMLS powder removal requires powder removal canals (PRCs) connecting internal voids to exterior. Cylindrical channels strategically placed.
notes: Analogous to lost-wax wax evacuation holes. PRCs reduce stiffness by ~10% average, optimized designs as low as 1.82%. No specific diameter given — need more sources for DMLS-specific evacuation hole size.

location.section: Weight and Wall Thickness — Test Results

excerpt: The 0.3 mm wall thickness has two major issues: the prints walls are not straight, but significantly concave... The casting is incompletely filled on one side. At 0.5 mm wall thickness, we see reliably complete fill, but there is some distortion and concavity. A wall thickness of 0.75 mm works well at this scale, with reduced distortion.
claim: Empirical test results: 0.3 mm walls fail (concave, incomplete fill). 0.5 mm walls cast completely but have distortion. 0.75 mm walls work well with minimal distortion.

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: THIS IS EMPIRICAL TEST DATA, not just a guideline. Gildform physically tested 0.3, 0.5, and 0.75 mm and documented results. 0.5 mm is the marginal threshold — casts but distorts. 0.75 mm is the production-safe minimum. This is the strongest evidence in the corpus.

excerpt: A bangle bracelet with width of 18 mm has a wall thickness of 0.9 mm. Version 1 with one small 3.5 mm hole cannot be cast. Version 2 with multiple larger access holes allows successful investment and casting.
claim: Hollow bangle: 0.9 mm walls, 18 mm width. Single 3.5 mm hole insufficient for casting. Multiple larger holes required for investment access.

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: Empirical: single hole is insufficient even at 3.5 mm. Investment must fill the hollow interior, not just drain resin. This is different from Materialise's 1.5 mm hole spec — Gildform needs larger/multiple holes because investment must enter, not just drain.

excerpt: Out-of-scope: Laser Engraving/cutting, Hinge-Making/clasps/spring mechanism, Interlocking parts/mechanical parts, Stone Setting, Some specialty assembly such as beading, Anything larger than 3in x 4in.
claim: Gildform out-of-scope: laser engraving, hinges, clasps, springs, interlocking/mechanical parts, stone setting, beading, parts larger than 3×4 inches (76×102 mm).

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: Stone setting is out of scope — important for Sculptura. Gildform casts only, no setting. Max size 76×102 mm is between Cooksongold (30×50×70) and Materialise (88×88×125).

excerpt: Wax ring: 3.25mm wide, 2.17mm thick, 22.03mm diameter. Silver cast: 3.23mm wide, 2.14mm thick, 21.92mm diameter. Barely any shrinkage in width and depth. About half a size smaller. After tapping round, the ring is the same size as wax.
claim: Empirical measurement: ring shrinkage was 0.02mm width (0.6%), 0.03mm thickness (1.4%), 0.11mm diameter (0.5%). Half ring size smaller. After tapping round, same size as wax.
notes: ACTUAL MEASURED shrinkage — much lower than documented ranges (0.5-1.4% vs 1.5-2.1%). Non-uniform: diameter shrank more than width. Tapping round recovered the size. This suggests shrinkage is geometry-dependent and may be partially recovered mechanically.

excerpt: How much smaller depends on the caster and what their shrinkage rate is (most common rate I've heard is 5-7%).
claim: Most common shrinkage rate heard from casters: 5-7%.
notes: This is much higher than other sources (1.5-2.1%). May include total shrinkage from wax to finished piece, or may be for mould casting (not lost-wax). Author notes 'there isn't that much shrinkage in lost wax casting' — the 5-7% may be for mould casting.

excerpt: I cut the seat of my settings to fit the stone exactly and leave a 1mm setting wall around.
claim: Setting wall thickness: 1 mm recommended for stone settings.
notes: Practitioner recommendation. Higher than eCadCam's 0.4-0.6 mm for bezel tops. This is the full wall, not just the top — thicker to allow for burr adjustment after shrinkage.

excerpt: For all practical purposes, through holes should have a minimum diameter of 0.5 mm, and that diameter only should be used for holes in very thin material. It is possible to cast smaller holes, but results may not be consistent in both printing and casting.
claim: Minimum through-hole diameter: 0.5 mm. Smaller holes are possible but inconsistent in printing and casting.

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: Gildform confirms 0.5 mm minimum, consistent with Cooksongold (src-0010). Recommends using a sphere-differenced pilot divot rather than a through-hole for small settings.

excerpt: 'Draft' is angling those walls and prongs so that they taper from a thicker base to a thinner top, and typically a 5-degree draft angle is sufficient to improve castability without being obtrusive. If the design supports it, a larger draft angle will always help.
claim: Draft angle of 5 degrees on walls and prongs improves castability. Larger draft angle always helps.

value.direction: taper from thicker base to thinner top

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: First source to give a specific draft angle number (5 degrees). Applies to walls and prongs specifically. Reduces investment stress between prong and wall, consistent with Formlabs guidance on negative-feature proportions.

excerpt: For jewelry models with fine detail, a layer height of 25 microns is recommended.
claim: Recommended layer height for fine jewelry: 25 microns.
notes: Confirms Sculpteo sterling silver (src-0003, 25 um) and Formlabs True Cast (src-0011, 25 and 50 microns). 25 microns is the fine-detail standard across multiple sources.

excerpt: We do not recommend engraving in the 3D Model as it may cause many quality issues in casting and finishing, resulting in a poor quality. If very fine engraving is desired, the best solution is for us to laser engrave or stamp the pieces. The height of the smallest letters is 1.5 mm, and the smallest letters of the ornate script tend to fail in both depths.
claim: Gildform does not recommend 3D model engraving; laser engraving preferred. Minimum letter height for survival: 1.5 mm. Engraving depth 0.3 mm shallower than 0.5 mm for small features.

scope.process: lost-wax casting from printed castable wax resin

notes: Gildform is the only source that explicitly recommends against 3d model engraving for casting. Other sources (cooksongold, sculpteo) give minimum dimensions but do not prohibit. The 1.5 mm minimum letter height for script survival aligns with sculpteo (src-0003, height 1.5 mm).

excerpt: sphere(radius | d=diameter), cube(size, center), cube([width,depth,height], center), cylinder(h,r|d,center), cylinder(h,r1|d1,r2|d2,center), polyhedron(points, faces, convexity), import(...), linear_extrude(...), rotate_extrude(...), surface(...)
claim: OpenSCAD 3D primitives: sphere, cube, cylinder (with two-radius form), polyhedron, import, linear_extrude, rotate_extrude, surface.
notes: Official cheatsheet confirms the full 3D primitive set and boolean operations available in OpenSCAD 2021.01. Resolution variables $fn (segment count), $fa (minimum angle), $fs (minimum segment length) control tessellation quality of curved surfaces.

excerpt: The minimum design thickness should be at least 0.40 mm and broad or flat areas should be at least 0.50 mm thick. If the final piece is required to be moulded for multiple copies, then should be at least 0.90 mm thick.
claim: Minimum design thickness 0.40 mm general, 0.50 mm for broad or flat areas, 0.90 mm if the piece will be moulded for multiple copies.

scope.process: lost-wax casting (3d printed or hand carved patterns)

notes: Fourth independent source on minimum thickness, and the most permissive general figure in the store; likely reflects casting-house repair capability rather than printability. Unreconciled with materialise 0.6-0.8, jfd 0.8, gildform 0.75 empirical pass.

excerpt: Raised text: designs must have a minimum width and spacing between letters of at least of 0.30 mm. Raised text should only have a maximum height of 0.50 mm.
claim: Raised text: minimum letter width and spacing 0.30 mm, maximum height 0.50 mm.
notes: Fourth source in the text conflict cluster. Max height 0.50 mm vs cooksongold 0.60 mm, sculpteo 1.50 mm, hi3dp 1.00 mm. Also recommends sans serif fonts, square angles, and avoiding curves that taper to a point.

excerpt: Recessed text: designs must have a minimum width and spacing between letters of at least of 0.30 mm. Recessed designs should be recessed to a maximum of 0.30 mm deep and no deeper than the width of the opening. If possible, draft or taper by 5-10 degrees so that the bottom of the impression is narrower than the opening.
claim: Recessed text: minimum width and spacing 0.30 mm, maximum depth 0.30 mm and no deeper than the opening width; draft taper 5-10 degrees recommended.
notes: Second source giving a specific draft angle (gildform: 5 degrees). Depth-bounded-by-opening rule mirrors the hole rule, consistently expressed across void types.

excerpt: The depth of the void should not exceed the width of the opening of the void. The maximum depth of a hole should not exceed 0.30 mm. Ensure that any holes are greater than 0.20 mm in diameter and do not have a depth larger than the diameter or opening of the hole.
claim: Void depth must not exceed opening width; hole depth capped at 0.30 mm; holes must exceed 0.20 mm diameter.
notes: Registration record: this page was captured in the original scrape pass and cited in the digest as 'morris and watson cad design guidelines' without a sources.jsonl record. Registered 2026-10-04 via direct re-scrape; all previously cited values verified present on the page.

source.title: How to Determine Ring Size: Tips and Ring Size Chart

excerpt: US and Canada size 3 = 14.1 mm inside diameter; size 6 = 16.5 mm; size 9 = 19.0 mm; size 12 = 21.4 mm; size 13 = 22.2 mm.
claim: US ring sizes 3 to 13 map to inside diameters 14.1 to 22.2 mm in 0.2 mm quarter-size steps.
notes: Replaces the unverified nominal table in benchmarks/size-family.scad. GIA rounds to one decimal (0.2 mm per quarter size). Size 9 corrects the prior 18.89 mm nominal value, which was flagged as suspect in the 2026-10-03 review; common two-decimal charts cite 19.10 mm for size 9, so a second chart source remains desirable before treating diameters as tight tolerances.
